description: Why Puritans saw the 1559 Settlement as unfinished — and how Elizabeth and Whitgift pushed back.
content_html:
Who Were the Puritans?

Puritans were not a single organised movement but a broad tendency within English Protestantism. They believed that the Reformation had not gone far enough — that the Church of England still retained too much Catholic ceremony, too many bishops with too much power, and insufficient emphasis on the Bible and preaching. The word “Puritan” was originally a term of abuse used by their opponents; they generally called themselves “the godly” or “the professors.” By the 1570s and 1580s, however, they had become a significant force in both Parliament and the Privy Council, making them a genuine political challenge to Elizabeth’s religious settlement.

The Puritan Challenge to the Settlement

Puritans wanted several reforms that Elizabeth refused to grant. They wanted to remove the remaining Catholic elements from worship — vestments, crucifixes, kneeling at Communion, the sign of the cross at baptism. They also wanted a reformed presbyterian church structure, replacing bishops with elected councils of elders (presbyters) as in Calvin’s Geneva. This was not merely a theological dispute: eliminating bishops would have removed the Queen’s control over the Church, since bishops were appointed by the Crown and enforced royal religious policy.

The leading intellectual voice for Presbyterianism in Elizabethan England was Thomas Cartwright, a Cambridge theologian who argued in the early 1570s that bishops had no basis in scripture and that the Church should be governed by elected elders. His views were too radical for Elizabeth’s government: Cartwright was eventually deprived of his Cambridge fellowship and spent years in exile and prison. Nevertheless, his ideas had wide influence among educated Protestants, including several members of the Privy Council.

Key Fact

Presbyterianism was a political as well as a religious threat. Bishops were appointed by the Crown and enforced royal religious policy. Replacing them with elected elders would have removed the Queen’s control over the Church — effectively creating an independent religious authority that could defy royal commands.

Puritan Opposition in Parliament

Puritan MPs attempted to push further reform through Parliament during the 1570s and 1580s. In 1571, Walter Strickland introduced a bill in the Commons to reform the prayer book along Puritan lines. Elizabeth had it withdrawn and banned Strickland from the Commons temporarily. In the Parliament of 1587, Anthony Cope introduced what became known as “Cope’s Bill and Book” — a proposal to replace the entire Book of Common Prayer with a Genevan (Calvinist) alternative and abolish episcopal church government. Elizabeth had the bill confiscated and imprisoned Cope and several other Puritan MPs in the Tower of London.

Puritans were not only in Parliament — several of Elizabeth’s most powerful councillors were sympathetic to their cause. Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, Francis Walsingham and (to some extent) William Cecil were all inclined towards stricter Protestantism. This gave Puritanism real influence within the government. However, these councillors supported Puritanism as a Protestant movement against Catholic threats rather than as a programme for dismantling the royal supremacy over the Church. When Puritan demands moved towards full presbyterianism, even sympathetic councillors tended to draw back.

The Marprelate Tracts, 1588–1589

The most provocative expression of Puritan opposition was the Marprelate Tracts, a series of anonymous satirical pamphlets published using a secret printing press in 1588 and 1589. Written under the pseudonym “Martin Marprelate,” these pamphlets attacked the bishops of the Church of England in savage, scurrilous terms — mocking them as corrupt, ignorant and unscriptural. The tracts were entertaining and widely read, but they shocked even some who were sympathetic to reform. The government tracked down the printing press; several men connected with the tracts were arrested and executed. The Marprelate affair hardened the government’s stance: Elizabeth became less willing to tolerate even moderate Puritan demands after this episode.

Government Response: Archbishop Whitgift

Elizabeth’s most effective weapon against the Puritan challenge was her appointment of Archbishop John Whitgift as Archbishop of Canterbury in 1583. Whitgift was a committed anti-Puritan who believed in firm episcopal discipline. He issued “Three Articles” requiring all clergy to subscribe to the royal supremacy, the prayer book and the Thirty-Nine Articles — the doctrinal foundation of the Church of England. Any clergy who refused were suspended. Whitgift used the Court of High Commission to discipline non-conforming clergy. His policies were controversial even within the government: William Cecil complained that his tactics were too harsh and compared them to the Spanish Inquisition. Nevertheless, they were broadly effective: the presbyterian movement within the Church was contained, and Puritanism was pushed towards the edges of the establishment.

Key Fact

Archbishop Whitgift (appointed 1583) required all clergy to subscribe to: the royal supremacy, the Book of Common Prayer, and the Thirty-Nine Articles. Clergy who refused were suspended. He used the Court of High Commission to enforce these requirements.

Historians debate how serious the Puritan threat really was. The traditional view presents Puritanism as a serious danger to the settlement. A revisionist view, associated with historians such as Peter Lake, argues that most Puritans were ‘church Puritans’ — loyal to Elizabeth and working within the Church, not against it — and that only a small minority were genuine separatists who rejected the Church entirely. On this reading, Elizabeth’s firm response was overkill that created more tension than it resolved. What is clear is that Puritanism was not suppressed permanently: it re-emerged as a much more powerful force in the seventeenth century, eventually contributing to the Civil War and the execution of Charles I in 1649.
exam_tip_html: For questions on the Puritan threat, focus on the specific vocabulary: presbyterianism, Thomas Cartwright, Marprelate Tracts, Archbishop Whitgift, Court of High Commission. For ‘Explain a cause’ questions, a strong answer would chain: Puritans demanded presbyterian church government → this threatened royal control over the Church → Elizabeth therefore refused and used Whitgift to enforce conformity. For 10-mark ‘Compare Interpretations’ questions, a typical pairing for this topic is the traditional view (Puritanism was a serious threat) versus the revisionist view (most Puritans were loyal ‘church Puritans’). Remember: explain WHY the interpretations differ, not just what each says.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Puritans wanted further reform of the Church of England — removing Catholic ceremony and replacing bishops with elected presbyterian elders. This threatened Elizabeth’s political control of the Church, so she consistently refused their demands.
  • Puritans used Parliament to push reform: Cope’s Bill and Book (1587) proposed replacing the entire prayer book and was suppressed. The Marprelate Tracts (1588–89) used satirical pamphlets to attack bishops, hardening the government’s response.
  • Elizabeth’s most effective response was appointing Archbishop Whitgift (1583), who used the Court of High Commission to enforce conformity and required clergy to subscribe to the royal supremacy, prayer book and Thirty-Nine Articles. The presbyterian movement within the Church was contained but not destroyed.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Puritan opposition to the Religious Settlement in Elizabethan England.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: a precise feature with supporting detail, e.g. Puritans argued that the Church should be governed by elected elders (presbyters) rather than bishops, because bishops had no basis in scripture (2 marks). Emerging: a vague feature (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Archbishop Whitgift's response to Puritanism.
practice_questions.marks: For each feature: Mastering: precise feature with accurate detail (2 marks). Emerging: simple feature without development (1 mark). Features may include: required all clergy to subscribe to the Three Articles (royal supremacy, prayer book, Thirty-Nine Articles); used the Court of High Commission to discipline non-conforming clergy; suspended clergy who refused to subscribe; appointed as Archbishop of Canterbury in 1583. Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of Elizabeth I's opposition to presbyterianism.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: detailed causal chain with evidence, e.g. Elizabeth opposed presbyterianism because bishops were appointed by the Crown and enforced royal religious policy — replacing them with elected elders would have removed the Queen's control over the Church, creating an independent religious authority with the potential power to defy royal commands. Secure: clear cause with some evidence. Developing: relevant cause with limited development. Emerging: simple point. Maximum 6 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Marprelate Tracts (1588–1589) for relations between Elizabeth I and Puritanism.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained analysis of significance at the time (hardened government's stance; led to arrests and executions; pushed Puritanism towards the edges of respectability) AND over time (demonstrated the limits of radical Puritanism; contributed to the later conflict between Crown and Puritans in the seventeenth century). Secure: clear explanation with specific evidence. Developing: some explanation. Emerging: simple points. Maximum 8 marks.

practice_questions.text: How useful is a pamphlet written by a Puritan MP arguing for greater religious reform for understanding the nature of the Puritan challenge to Elizabeth?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: integrates content, provenance (a Puritan MP — committed reformer, wants change; may overstate urgency) and contextual knowledge (Puritan MPs were real; Cope's Bill and Book shows the parliamentary dimension; but most Puritans worked within the Church) to give a substantiated judgement. Secure: addresses two elements. Developing: mainly describes source. Emerging: simple comment. Maximum 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: 'Elizabeth I successfully dealt with the Puritan challenge to the Religious Settlement.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: argues for (Whitgift contained presbyterianism; Cope's Bill suppressed; no Puritan rebellion; settlement survived the reign) AND against (Puritanism was not destroyed; it re-emerged in the seventeenth century; the Marprelate affair showed how difficult control was; some councillors were sympathetic to reform) before a substantiated overall judgement. Secure: both sides with evidence and conclusion. Developing: one-sided. Emerging: simple. Maximum 12 marks.

knowledge_checks.q: What system of church government did Puritans want to replace the episcopal (bishop) system with?
options: A presbyterian system of elected elders

knowledge_checks.q: What was the purpose of the Marprelate Tracts (1588–1589)?
options: To defend the Elizabethan church settlement against Catholics
To attack bishops in anonymous satirical pamphlets, demanding further reform
To argue for England's war with Spain on religious grounds
To support Mary Queen of Scots' claim to the throne

knowledge_checks.q: Archbishop _____ was appointed by Elizabeth in 1583 to enforce conformity and discipline Puritan clergy.
Thomas Cartwright argued in the 1570s that _____ had no basis in scripture and should be replaced by elected elders.
Match each element of Elizabeth's response to Puritanism to its description:
right: Appointed in 1583 to enforce conformity in the Church of England
The ecclesiastical court used to discipline non-conforming clergy
Required clergy to subscribe to royal supremacy, prayer book and Thirty-Nine Articles

flashcard_questions.q: What did Puritans want that Elizabeth refused to grant?
flashcard_questions.a: Further reform: removal of Catholic ceremony and replacement of bishops with presbyterian elected elders.

flashcard_questions.q: Why was presbyterianism a political threat to Elizabeth?
flashcard_questions.a: Removing bishops would have ended royal control of the Church, as bishops were appointed by the Crown.
A Cambridge theologian who argued bishops were unscriptural and advocated presbyterian church government.
A Puritan MP's proposal to replace the Book of Common Prayer and abolish bishops — suppressed by Elizabeth.
Anonymous satirical pamphlets attacking bishops, published on a secret press, that hardened the government's response.

flashcard_questions.q: When was Archbishop Whitgift appointed and what was his significance?
flashcard_questions.a: 1583; he enforced conformity using the Three Articles and the Court of High Commission.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Whitgift's Three Articles require clergy to subscribe to?
flashcard_questions.a: The royal supremacy, the Book of Common Prayer, and the Thirty-Nine Articles.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the Court of High Commission?
flashcard_questions.a: The ecclesiastical court Whitgift used to discipline Puritan clergy who refused to conform.

flashcard_questions.q: Which of Elizabeth's senior councillors were sympathetic to Puritanism?
flashcard_questions.a: Robert Dudley (Earl of Leicester) and Francis Walsingham.

flashcard_questions.q: Why did Puritanism not permanently disappear in Elizabeth's reign?
flashcard_questions.a: It was contained but not destroyed; it re-emerged powerfully in the seventeenth century.

flashcard_questions.q: The Puritan challenge to the settlement was mainly expressed through _____ and through opposition within Parliament.
flashcard_questions.a: Theological argument (presbyterianism, e.g. Thomas Cartwright) and pamphlets (Marprelate Tracts).

glossary_terms.definition: Protestant reformers who believed the Church of England retained too many Catholic practices after the 1559 Settlement and demanded a purer form of worship and a reformed church structure.
A system of church government based on elected assemblies of elders (presbyters) rather than bishops, advocated by Puritans as a replacement for the episcopal hierarchy.
Cambridge theologian and leading advocate of presbyterian church government in Elizabethan England, who argued bishops were unscriptural.
A series of anonymous satirical pamphlets published secretly in 1588–1589 that attacked bishops in scurrilous terms, hardening the government's response to Puritanism.
Archbishop of Canterbury from 1583 who used the Court of High Commission to discipline Puritan clergy and enforce conformity to the Church of England.
The ecclesiastical court used by Archbishop Whitgift to enforce conformity and discipline non-conforming Puritan clergy.
